coverage: A nationwide research directory, not a complete or current legal inventory. The source uses AI-assisted research and mixed official/news evidence. An imported date is not an independent verification date. Multiple instruments may describe one jurisdiction; aliases may occur. Statewide restrictions and permanent bans are not exhaustively covered. No entry does not establish no moratorium.

records.basis: Ordinance No. 26-20, City of Houston, Alaska (introduced 2026-09-10; public hearing/vote scheduled 2026-10-08)
records.detail: Pending as of 2026-09-23. Ordinance 26-20, establishing a temporary two-year moratorium on the acceptance, processing, approval, or issuance of permits as well as construction, establishment, and operation of data centers within Houston city limits, was introduced on the council's September 10, 2026 consent agenda; a public hearing and council action vote are scheduled for October 8, 2026. The introduction followed an August 13, 2026 meeting at which a differently drafted anti-data-center ordinance failed 4-2, and coincides with council opposition to a proposed ~20,000-acre state land transfer to AIDEA (Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority) near Houston that could host data centers.

records.dateNote: 2026-08-11 (Board of Supervisors adopted an addendum-item resolution at its regular meeting, 3-2 vote)
records.term: 120 days from adoption (2026-08-11 to approximately 2026-12-09), to give county staff time to finalize a zoning code text amendment establishing data-center-specific regulations; Supervisor Heinz's floor amendment provided the moratorium could return to the board for possible extension before the 120-day limit.
records.basis: Resolution adopted by the Pima County Board of Supervisors at its August 11, 2026 regular meeting, added as an addendum item at the request of Board Chair Jennifer Allen (District 3); no separately reported resolution number located in captured sources.
records.detail: Active as of 2026-09-23. 120-day moratorium on the acceptance/issuance of new data center permits in unincorporated Pima County, adopted 3-2 (Supervisors Christy and Scott dissenting) on 2026-08-11 and running to approximately 2026-12-09, while Development Services finalizes a zoning code text amendment. The department is seeking public comment (online survey; a September 28, 2026 open house; proposed rules going to the Planning and Zoning Commission on October 28, 2026) on a related, permanent zoning code amendment that would define data centers (facilities using more than 20 MW), require closed-loop cooling, and set review/design standards; that permanent amendment is expected in December 2026, around when the moratorium runs out.

correction.text: The source confuses the August 11 direction to draft a measure with adoption. The official record marks Resolution 2026-56 approved September 22, 2026. Use the reviewed Pima County case; do not rely on the source’s August adoption date or calculated December endpoint.

records.dateNote: 2026-06-16 (Carroll County Quorum Court unanimous adoption of Emergency Ordinance 2026-17)
records.term: Immediate 12-month moratorium from adoption
records.basis: Emergency Ordinance 2026-17
records.detail: Active as of 2026-09-23. The 12-month emergency moratorium (Ordinance 2026-17), unanimously adopted by the Quorum Court on 2026-06-16 and effective immediately, remains in force with no reported repeal, extension, or replacement; its 365-day term runs through 2027-06-16. Corroborated by a second independent local news source (the Eureka Springs Independent's contemporaneous meeting report) beyond the original KY3 broadcast story, and by three specialty policy trackers (ServerCountry, SAVRN, AI GridWatch) that separately cite the ordinance number and June 16 vote. A complete signed county copy of the ordinance was still not located on the county's website or in Municode as of 2026-09-23, so the underlying record remains multiple independent news accounts rather than a primary ordinance document. [VERIFY] [VERIFY primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.65 in the 2026-07 refresh]

records.term: One year or until specific land-use standards were developed, whichever occurred first
records.basis: Ordinance 1515, "An Ordinance Imposing a Temporary Moratorium on Data Centers and Crypto Mining Facilities in the City of Harrison, Arkansas"
records.detail: Repealed; Harrison City Council voted 6-2 to repeal Ordinance 1515 at a specially called meeting on Tuesday, 2023-11-28, on a motion by Council Member Mitch Magness, seconded by Council Member Joel Williams (councilors Jeremy Ragland and Wayne Cone voted no). City Attorney Nancy Cartwright recommended repeal as a litigation precaution tied to a federal court matter involving Green Digital and the state's data-mining protections; the council also amended its noise ordinance the same night (Ordinance 1516). No separate numbered repeal ordinance for Ordinance 1515 itself was identified in the Harrison Daily Times' contemporaneous account of the meeting, and the city's own ordinance/clerk portal (harrisonar.gov) is behind a bot-protection challenge page that could not be bypassed to check the clerk's ordinance index directly.

records.detail: Active as of 2026-09-23. The July 16, 2026 City Council agenda (Item 3, New Business) confirms the ordinance considered and adopted that night was titled 'An Ordinance Imposing a Temporary Moratorium on the Acceptance, Processing and Approval of Applications for the Development, Construction, or Siting of Data Centers Within the Incorporated Areas of the City of Russellville... Establishing a Temporary Committee...', sponsored by Council Member Justin Keller; River Valley Radio and a Citizen Portal meeting summary confirm the council amended the sponsor's original 18-month proposal down to six months (6-2) and then adopted the amended ordinance (6-2). The resulting ad hoc committee (also reported as the 'Data Center Research Committee' / 'Zoning and Land Use Amendments Committee') was seated and was still actively meeting as of an Aug. 18, 2026 River Valley Radio report, with no report found of the moratorium being lifted or repealed early. The signed ordinance's assigned number, precise effective date, and sunset date still were not located in the city's online ordinance archive or on Municode as of 2026-09-23. KPBS ('the city of Imperial has also temporarily frozen all data center development through May 2027') and Hoodline both independently confirm this as of August 2026, and no further change was found through 2026-09-23. This is unrelated to, and unaffected by, the Imperial County Superior Court's September 2026 order setting aside the separate Imperial County Board of Supervisors moratorium (ca-imperial-county-2026), which governs unincorporated county land only.

records.detail: Rescinded by court order as of 2026-09-23. Imperial County Superior Court Judge Jeffrey B. Jones entered judgment 2026-09-04 in favor of developer Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC, finding neither Ordinance 1616 (the original moratorium) nor Ordinance 1618 (its ~10-month-15-day extension) made the causal finding of a 'current and immediate threat to public health, safety, or welfare' required by Gov. Code section 65858. A peremptory writ of mandate issued 2026-09-11 directs the County and Board of Supervisors to set aside both ordinances and stop using them to withhold, suspend, or refuse data-center permits. The County has said (per KYMA, 2026-09-22) it is working on a new moratorium addressing the court's concerns; no replacement had been adopted as of 2026-09-23. The Data Center Advisory Committee, created alongside the moratorium, continues to meet (inaugural meeting 2026-09-17) and is unaffected by the ruling. Separately, a different judge (L. Brooks Anderholt) has ordered a full CEQA environmental review of the underlying data center project in a related case, so the project itself remains stalled notwithstanding the moratorium's invalidation.

records.detail: Active as of 2026-09-23 (moderate confidence). The Legislation Committee gave a Favorable Report on 2026-08-04 and the item (LM-2026-0285) was on the full Board of Alders' September 8, 2026 agenda. Yale Daily News reported (headline and lede snippet) that the Board voted unanimously that Tuesday to adopt the 12-month data center moratorium. This could not be independently corroborated: the Yale Daily News article itself returned a bot-detection (Kasada) challenge on both a direct and a browser-mode fetch, so only the search-engine snippet could be read; New Haven Independent, which had covered every earlier stage of this item in detail, published no follow-up story on the Sept. 8 vote; and the official September 8, 2026 Board of Alders meeting agenda (fetched directly from newhaven-ct.legistar.com) groups LM-2026-0285 together with several unrelated items under a 'Legislation. Leave to withdraw' heading, which -- taken literally -- would mean the Legislation Committee's report on this batch recommended withdrawal rather than passage. This agenda-formatting ambiguity is inconsistent with the item's own recorded 8/4/2026 'Favorable Report' status and could reflect a template/carryover artifact in how the city's agenda software groups items, rather than an actual disposition of LM-2026-0285 specifically. Because no direct, unambiguous confirmation of the final vote result could be obtained, this decision is recorded with moderate rather than high confidence.

records.detail: Replaced, as of 2026-09-23. The January 16, 2026 M-2 Data Center Ordinance (conditional use in M-2 industrial zoning, with 200-foot setbacks, 400-foot setbacks for noise-generating buildings, up to 200-foot buffers, 55/45 dB noise limits, and closed-loop cooling requirements) remains in force but is under active legal challenge: 17 Jones County residents filed a declaratory-judgment lawsuit in February 2026 seeking to void the ordinance on due-process and Georgia Zoning Procedures Law grounds; the county filed a motion to dismiss in March 2026, and as of a Jones County Development Authority meeting reported by The Jones County News, the judge had not yet set a hearing on that motion, with the attorney estimating a 2027 timeline. records.detail: Still in effect as of 2026-09-23, event-based: the July 21 second reading never occurred as planned. Court Chair Voegele ruled the Fiscal Court's 2026-08-24 special-called meeting void because the court failed to approve its own agenda, so the item restarted. On 2026-09-01 the Fiscal Court reconsidered and unanimously adopted substantive revisions to the draft regulations (still numbered KOC 26-920-5): striking all references to 'large'/'hyperscale' data centers while adding a 10 MW maximum power-capacity cap (effectively banning hyperscale projects), raising the square-footage cap for 'medium' data centers to 110,000 sq ft, and requiring two weeks' advance notice to property owners within 1,000 ft of a proposed site's neighborhood meeting. County Attorney D. Berry Baxter, backed by outside zoning counsel and the Kentucky Association of Counties, concluded KRS 100.211(8)'s 90-day deadline for zoning MAP amendments does not apply to this zoning TEXT amendment, so no statutory deadline forces a vote. The Fiscal Court's public hearing and final (second-reading) vote on KOC 26-920-5 is now calendared for 2026-10-06, after this research date. The moratorium (KOC 25-910-508, extended by KOC 25-910-520 'until data center regulations are approved') has no fixed end date -- it remains the operative instrument until that vote occurs (or another statutory event ends it), consistent with an Aug. 19, 2026 news report confirming the moratorium 'remains in place' pending the Fiscal Court's next action.

records.basis: Resolution 30-2024-03 (Sept. 12, 2024 moratorium). Superseded in substance by a County Commission resolution adopted 2026-09-10 (4-1 vote, Commissioner Tokach dissenting over a tonal-noise feasibility concern) that added a Data Center Standards section to the Morton County Land Use Code, following Planning & Zoning Commission review at its Feb. 25, March 25, April 22, May 27, and July 22, 2026 meetings, a subcommittee process (June-August 2026), and a P&Z recommendation of approval on Aug. 26, 2026.
records.detail: Replaced as of 2026-09-23. The County Commission adopted a Data Center Standards section for the Morton County Land Use Code on 2026-09-10 (4-1), and the county's website states this final draft 'has been incorporated into the Morton County Land Use Code.' The standards set noise limits (noise-producing equipment generally at least three-quarters of a mile from an occupied home), require closed-loop cooling, and set setback, water/power-use, road, emergency-planning, and reclamation-bond requirements (with a waiver path if a former data center site is repurposed). Per the Bismarck Tribune's Sept. 11, 2026 report, the Planning & Zoning Director stated a separate notice period was required before the Commission could formally vote to lift the underlying moratorium resolution itself (since it was adopted by resolution), and she expected that vote at the Commission's next meeting after Sept. 10; no report of that specific repeal vote was found as of 2026-09-23. No data center application is currently pending in the county's own (non-extraterritorial) jurisdiction; a separate proposed Stark Power data-center/gas-generation project in north Mandan falls within the City of Mandan's extraterritorial area, not Morton County's jurisdiction.

Grube) that Ashville's fiscal officer improperly refused to certify a citizen referendum petition against Resolution 06-2026 because the emergency declaration was not adequately justified; the Pickaway County Board of Elections then voted unanimously to place the referendum on the 2026-11-03 general-election ballot. Village Council subsequently introduced Resolution 16-2026 to repeal Resolution 06-2026 outright and moot the referendum; a 2026-09-08 motion to waive the second and third readings and pass it immediately fell short of the five-vote supermajority required (final tally of 4 in favor, after Mayor Clark broke an initial 3-3 tie, which the council's own rules held insufficient), and at the 2026-09-21 meeting Council instead advanced the repeal to a third reading scheduled for 2026-10-05. records.detail: Pending as of 2026-09-23. records.term: Until a comprehensive health and safety review is complete, per the posted draft order; no fixed term confirmed
records.basis: Order of Austin County, Texas, Regarding Battery Energy Storage Systems and Data Centers Health and Safety Review, adopted by the Commissioners Court on 2026-07-27 under Texas Health and Safety Code section 121.003 and Texas Local Government Code section 352.016, among other authorities. The signed, executed order was located directly on austincounty.com (distinct from the earlier unsigned draft). It suspends county permit, plan-review, and inspection approvals for BESS and data center construction in unincorporated areas until a 'Comprehensive Health and Safety Review' (covering fire/life-safety, cybersecurity/foreign-adversary equipment verification tied to the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act and the Governor's Prohibited Technologies List, and an Energy Development Zone siting study) is complete, with the Commissioners Court retaining sole discretion over when that review is finished. It requires County Fire Marshal plan review/approval and an independent third-party engineering evaluation before construction, and authorizes the County's legal counsel to seek injunctive relief against violators.
records.detail: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Commissioners Court unanimously adopted the signed order on 2026-07-27 following the July 13, 2026 public hearing; KWHI (2026-07-28) independently confirms the unanimous vote and describes the order's scope (equipment-manufacturer audits, an Energy Development Zone siting study by the County Fire Marshal and County Engineer, and injunctive-relief enforcement authority). No fixed term applies; the order remains in effect, by its own terms, until the Commissioners Court (in consultation with the County Fire Marshal) determines the Comprehensive Health and Safety Review is complete. No repeal, rescission, or completion of the review was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. KWHI notes Austin County is 'the second county in Texas to adopt a moratorium of this nature,' after Hill County (which later rescinded its moratorium following a developer lawsuit; see the existing tx-hill-county-2026 row).

The Resolution 26-R-042 deferral remains in force, running 8 months from its July 21, 2026 adoption (to approximately 2027-03-21) or until Council takes final action on comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002, whichever occurs first. On August 18, 2026 the City Council separately and unanimously adopted a zoning ordinance amendment that removes data centers from by-right development, requires a conditional use permit for all future data center proposals in the M-1/M-2 industrial districts, and prohibits data centers from drawing groundwater; this closed a loophole that could have let a data center proceed administratively despite the moratorium, but it is a permanent zoning change layered on top of, not a replacement for, the still-active Resolution 26-R-042 deferral. The zoning change was prompted partly by Praetorian Fund's August 2026 purchase of the Frank Williams Farm Tract (Coastal Virginia Commerce Park); because that site does not connect to public utilities, city officials confirmed the moratorium independently applies to it. No repeal, extension, or expiration of the moratorium itself was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
